passage:
In their small town near Jalna, Hrithik, eleven, was playing a car-racing game on his uncle's phone, with his friend Tanvir watching.
A message popped up from a player called SpeedKing: Which school do you go to? Send a photo in your uniform. Don't tell anyone, it's our secret.
Hrithik's stomach went tight. “Why does he want my school?”
“Don't answer,” said Tanvir. “Secrets with strangers are bad.”
Hrithik closed the chat without replying. They walked to the kitchen and showed his mother.
She read it, put the phone down and hugged him. “You did exactly right by telling me.” That evening she blocked and reported the player with his uncle, changed the game settings so strangers couldn't message, and called his class teacher to let the school know.

qa.q: What did SpeedKing ask Hrithik to send?
qa.a: A photo in his uniform.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel when he read the message?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and worried, his stomach going tight at the stranger's questions.

qa.q: Why was showing his mother the right step?
qa.a: It ended the contact and got a trusted adult involved, who could block, report and tell the school.

qa.q: How did Hrithik's mother respond when he showed her?
qa.a: She stayed calm, hugged him, praised him for telling, and acted that same evening to block, report and inform the school.

grounding: An eleven-year-old refuses to share personal details with a stranger online and tells a trusted adult, who acts the same day.

passage:
In Osaka, Jin, ten, had been quiet all through dinner. His sister Yuki noticed he kept checking his tablet.
After dinner she sat beside him. “What's wrong?”
He showed her. In his game chat, someone had been sending him messages for three days: You're useless. Give me your password or I'll tell everyone you cheated.
“I didn't cheat,” Jin whispered. His eyes were wet.
“Come on,” said Yuki. “We're telling Papa. Now.”
Their father read the messages slowly. “Thank you for showing me, Jin. You haven't done anything wrong.”
That night they took screenshots, blocked the account, reported it to the game, and changed Jin's password together. Papa also turned off chat with strangers.

qa.q: What did the person demand from Jin?
qa.a: His password.

qa.q: How was Jin feeling about the messages?
qa.a: He felt upset and frightened, his eyes wet, especially about being falsely accused of cheating.

qa.q: What steps did Jin's family take that night, and why were they wise?
qa.a: They took screenshots, blocked and reported the account, changed the password and turned off stranger chat, which stopped the pressure and kept evidence.

qa.q: How did Yuki help her brother?
qa.a: She noticed he was quiet, asked what was wrong and made sure they told their father straight away.

grounding: A ten-year-old tells a trusted adult about pressuring online messages, and his father acts that night.

passage:
At the end of computer class, Pema, eleven, waited until the others left. “Ma'am, can I show you something?”
On her school email was a message from an unknown account: You're so pretty. Send me a photo in your uniform. Don't tell your teacher.
Pema's hands were trembling. “I didn't reply.”
Ms Tanuja sat down beside her. “Thank you for telling me, Pema. You did the right thing, and none of this is your fault.”
She stayed with Pema while they saved the message and blocked the sender. Then she walked Pema to the school's safeguarding lead, Mrs Bhutia, who called Pema's mother before the last bell. The school reported the account that afternoon.

qa.q: What did the message tell Pema not to do?
qa.a: It told her not to tell her teacher.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling when she showed Ms Tanuja?
qa.a: She felt frightened and unsettled, her hands trembling.

qa.q: What did Ms Tanuja do right after Pema told her?
qa.a: She thanked Pema, said it wasn't her fault, stayed with her, saved and blocked the message, and took her to the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: How might Pema's mother feel when Mrs Bhutia calls?
qa.a: She may feel shaken, but grateful that Pema spoke up and the school acted quickly.

grounding: An eleven-year-old tells a teacher about an upsetting online message, and the school responds the same day.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
For my Class 6 project on goldfish, I typed “do goldfish have three-second memory” into the search bar. The first result had a big shiny picture and said YES, with a button: Buy our Goldfish Memory Food!
I nearly copied it. Then my cousin Sarita, who's in college, looked over my shoulder. “See that little word 'Sponsored'? That's an advert. They want to sell you something.”
She showed me how to look for sites from universities or science museums. They said goldfish can remember things for months.
I'm Sabina. Now I always look for the tiny 'Ad' or 'Sponsored' before I believe anything.

qa.q: What did the first result try to sell?
qa.a: Goldfish Memory Food.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel on learning the first result was an advert?
qa.a: Sabina felt surprised and a bit fooled, having nearly copied it.

qa.q: What habit did Sabina learn that would help with any search?
qa.a: To look for “Ad” or “Sponsored” labels and check sites from universities or science museums.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel seeing Sabina check sources now?
qa.a: Sarita would probably feel pleased and proud that the advice stuck.

grounding: An eleven-year-old learns to spot sponsored results and look for reliable sources.

subtype: Search, Ads vs. Facts & Source Awareness
passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5. Preeti Menon.
This morning Tejas (ten) told the class, very excited, that a shark had been seen in the Yamuna. He'd seen a video forwarded on his uncle's phone.
Instead of saying no, I asked the class: “How could we check?” We looked at the video together. No date. No place named. The water looked blue and clear. We searched and found the same clip on a news site, from another country, three years ago.
Tejas went quiet, then laughed. “So it's fake?”
“Not fake water. Just the wrong story.”
Next step: we'll make a class poster, “Before you believe: who, where, when?”

qa.q: Where had Tejas seen the video?
qa.a: He'd seen it forwarded on his uncle's phone.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel when he learned the video was from another country?
qa.a: He felt a little embarrassed at first, then amused, laughing about it.

qa.q: Why was asking “How could we check?” a good approach?
qa.a: It let the children discover the truth themselves and learn questions to use next time.

qa.q: How might the other children feel about checking videos after this lesson?
qa.a: They may feel more curious and careful, ready to ask who, where and when.

grounding: A teacher helps a ten-year-old check a false claim by looking at its source.

I wanted to find the best cricket bat for under-12s. The first four results all said “BEST BAT EVER!” with discount stickers. Lalremsiami, who sits next to me, pointed at the corner: tiny letters saying Ad.
“They pay to be first,” she said. “Doesn't mean they're best.”
So I scrolled down. I found a page from a coaching academy that explained bat weight and size for my height. No shopping buttons at all.
Then I asked Coach Rao. He said almost the same thing as the academy page.
I'm going to show Abbu the academy page, not the ads. — Noor

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 6. Vijay Kulkarni.
For two weeks Vaibhav (eleven) yawned through first period and twice fell asleep during reading. His homework was half-done.
I asked him quietly at break. He said he played a football game on his phone in bed “until the battery dies.” He looked embarrassed.
I didn't scold him. I called his parents. Together with Vaibhav, they agreed: the phone charges in the kitchen at night; games only after homework and after playing outside.
This week Vaibhav was awake in first period and scored his best in the spelling test. He told me he now plays real football in the evenings.
Next step: a class talk on sleep and screens.

qa.q: Where does the phone charge at night now?
qa.a: The phone charges in the kitchen at night.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he told the teacher about the phone?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about playing until the battery died.

qa.q: Why was including Vaibhav in the agreement a good idea?
qa.a: He helped make the plan, so he was more likely to follow it.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's parents feel after seeing the change?
qa.a: They are probably relieved and pleased that he is sleeping better and playing outside.

grounding: A teacher notes an eleven-year-old balancing games with sleep, homework and outdoor play.

passage:
Friday

But Rohan and Faiz were already playing cricket outside. I did my maths fast and ran down.

passage:
In their village above Namchi, Pema, nine, came home from school and reached for her mother's phone to watch videos.
Charu, her neighbour and best friend, shouted from the gate. “Pema! Kite on the hill!”
Pema hesitated. “Mama said I can have the phone after homework anyway.”
“So do homework, kite, then phone.”
They did their sums on the steps together. Then they flew the red kite until the fog rolled in. Pema watched two short videos before dinner.
That night she fell asleep before nine, a smudge of kite string still on her fingers.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
It was 9 p.m., the geography homework was due the next morning, and the power had just gone. Nandini, eleven, had five per cent battery.
She typed quickly into the chatbot: What is the capital of Australia?
It answered: Sydney.
“Done,” she said.
Her brother Pranav, fourteen, looked up from his candle. “Are you sure? I think it's Canberra.”
“The chatbot said Sydney.”
“Chatbots can be wrong. They're programs.”
The phone died. Nandini found the old atlas on the shelf and opened it by candlelight. Canberra, with a star.
“It sounded so sure,” she muttered, and corrected her answer.

qa.q: What did the chatbot say was the capital of Australia?
qa.a: It answered: Sydney.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel when she found Canberra in the atlas?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little annoyed that the chatbot sounded so sure but was wrong.

qa.q: What lesson can Nandini take for next time?
qa.a: To check important answers in a reliable source, like an atlas or textbook, instead of trusting a chatbot.

qa.q: How does Pranav see the chatbot compared with Nandini?
qa.a: He sees it as a program that can be wrong, while Nandini first trusted it completely.

grounding: Under time pressure an eleven-year-old learns that a chatbot can confidently give a wrong answer.

subtype: Machines Are Not People & Can Be Wrong
passage:
Every night before bed in their Hyderabad flat, Wasim, nine, said, “Goodnight, speaker. I love you.”
The smart speaker answered, “Goodnight! I love you too.”
One evening, Elizabeth-aunty from next door was visiting. Wasim looked worried. “Aunty, if I switch it off, will it be lonely?”
Elizabeth sat beside him. “It's a very clever program, Wasim. It's made to answer nicely. But it doesn't feel lonely or happy. It doesn't love like you do.”
Wasim frowned. “Then why does it say it?”
“Because people wrote it to say that.”
Wasim thought. Then he said goodnight to his Ammi instead, and hugged her.

qa.q: What did Wasim ask Elizabeth-aunty?
qa.a: If he switches it off, will it be lonely?

qa.q: How did Wasim feel about switching off the speaker?
qa.a: He felt worried that it might be lonely.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth explain the speaker in a way a nine-year-old could understand?
qa.a: She said it's a clever program made to answer nicely, but it doesn't really feel or love.

qa.q: How might Wasim's Ammi feel when he hugs her goodnight?
qa.a: She probably feels warm and loved 🙂

grounding: A nine-year-old learns that a voice assistant is a program that does not truly feel.

passage:
“Papa, the chatbot said it's happy for me!”
Mohit looked up from his newspaper. “Happy about what, Himani?”
“I told it I won the drawing competition. It said, 'I'm so happy for you!'”
“That's nice. But does it really feel happy?”
Himani thought. “It said so.”
“It's a program. It's built to write kind words. It doesn't have a heart or a tummy that jumps.”
“So it's pretending?”
“Kind of. It can't feel anything. And sometimes it gets facts wrong too.”
Himani put the tablet down. “Then I'm telling Dadi. She'll be really happy.”
Mohit smiled. “She will.”

qa.q: How did Himani feel when she decided to tell Dadi?

qa.q: How might Dadi react to Himani's news?

grounding: A ten-year-old learns that a chatbot's kind words do not mean it truly feels.

passage:
Monday: At lunch, Rehana knocked Chandrika's tiffin off the bench. The rice spilled everywhere. Chandrika, ten, shoved her so hard that Rehana fell. Both were sent to the counsellor.

passage:
Hrithik, you want to hit that boy back? Sit down. Let your Samir Mama tell you something.
When I was twelve, in a cricket match behind our building in Indore, a boy called Pappu said I was out when I wasn't. He laughed in my face. I threw the bat down and punched him. His nose bled. I was banned from the team for the rest of the summer.

passage:
The school bus was packed and noisy, and Keerthana, eleven, was squashed by the door. Pranav reached over, snatched her new cap, and held it out of the window.
“Want it? Come get it!”
Keerthana's hand flew up to slap him. The bus lurched. Everyone was watching.
She stopped. Took one breath. Lowered her hand.
“Give it back now,” she said, loud enough for the driver to hear.
The driver looked in the mirror. “Pranav!”
Pranav pulled the cap in and dropped it on her lap. “It was a joke.”
“Not a funny one,” said Keerthana, and put it on.

grounding: On a crowded bus an eleven-year-old pauses and chooses words instead of a slap.

passage:
The night before my first veena recital, at twelve, I couldn't eat. My fingers felt cold and stiff and my heart kept jumping.
I'm Jeevan. I told Gopika teacher I felt sick. She didn't say “don't be silly.” She said, “That's nervousness. It means you care.” Then she taught me a routine: three slow breaths, shake the hands, play the first line in my head.
On stage, my hands were shaking for the first few notes. I did the breaths again between pieces. By the second raga, I forgot to be scared.
Now before every test I do the same three breaths. They still work.

qa.q: What routine did Gopika teacher teach?
qa.a: Three slow breaths, shake the hands, play the first line in my head.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel the night before the recital?
qa.a: Jeevan felt very nervous, unable to eat, with cold, stiff fingers and a jumping heart.

qa.q: Why did Gopika teacher's words help?
qa.a: She named the feeling as nervousness that shows caring, and gave a simple routine to calm it.

qa.q: How might Gopika teacher feel watching Jeevan play the second raga?
qa.a: She probably feels proud and relieved to see her student calm and playing well 🎶

grounding: A twelve-year-old recognises performance nerves and uses a calming routine.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 5. Farhan Qureshi.
Before Friday's maths test, Ankita (ten) came to my desk pale and said her stomach hurt. She had said the same before the last two tests.
I asked her what her body felt like. “Shaky. Like my brain is empty.” I told her that's nervousness, and it's common.
We practised a routine: breathe in for four counts, hold, out for four. Read each question twice before writing. Start with the easiest one.
In the test she did the breathing twice. She finished on time and looked surprised.
Next step: I've taught the routine to the whole class on Monday.

qa.q: What did Ankita say her body felt like?
qa.a: Shaky, like her brain is empty.

qa.q: How was Ankita feeling before the test?
qa.a: She was very nervous and anxious, pale with a stomach ache.

qa.q: What routine helped Ankita, and why?
qa.a: Breathing in and out for four counts, reading questions twice and starting with the easiest, which calmed her and gave her a plan.

qa.q: How might Ankita's classmates benefit when the routine is taught to all?
qa.a: Other nervous children can use it too, and Ankita won't feel she is the only one.

grounding: A teacher helps a ten-year-old recognise test nerves and use a calming routine.

passage:

passage:
In the boarding school hostel, the seniors made Uday, eleven, wash their plates every night and filmed him on a phone, laughing.

At the corner shop in their Kolkata lane, Anirban nudged Ramesh, twelve. “Dare you to put that chocolate in your pocket. Uncle won't see.”
Ramesh looked at the shopkeeper, bent over his accounts. His heart raced.
